newsitem.title: UK: Gas to knock heavy fuel off European power throne.
newsitem.headline: Gas to knock heavy fuel off European power throne.

text.p: A 30 percent drop in the price of heavy fuel oil in Europe since December may signal a long-term downward realignment of its value against crude, said oil traders and analysts.
While weather has been a key to the recent price falls, underlying demand for fuel oil will keep declining as power stations continue the dash to burn gas.
"Although refinery closures this year mean less supply, it will not be enough to overcome falls in demand," said one oil analyst who monitors global demand trends.
High sulphur fuel oil in Rotterdam currently stands almost $6 a barrel beneath the value of benchmark dated Brent crude, compared to just a dollar under early last year.
Two years ago fuel oil was even worth more than crude.
Total European fuel oil demand fell by 1.6 percent in 1996, the IEA said, with losses in the UK, Germany and Italy partly offset by rising demand in Turkey and Scandinavian countries.
Ongoing programmes to close some European refineries and to upgrade others will remove some fuel oil from the market this year.
But analysts declined to forecast the precise extent of this.

Two new gas lines from Algeria - the Transmed pipeline expansion to Italy and the Maghreb pipe to Spain and Portugal - have been inaugurated in the last few months, and will displace fuel oil demand in those three countries.

Data published this week in trade newsletter Staffetta Quotidiana forecast that Italian state utility ENEL, accounting for around 90 percent of Italy's fuel purchases, would buy just 19.5 million tonnes of fuel this year, a 13 percent fall from 1996.
Perhaps more important for prices is a 21 percent drop in the amount of fuel ENEL is expected to import from the international market this year.
Most of the power shortfall in Italy will be met by increased gas-fired production by independent power producers, and greater imports of electricity from France, Staffetta said.
Provisional data from the International Energy Agency (IEA) shows dizzying falls in fuel use last year in most major European economies.

For instance, Germany's fuel consumption was down 9.5 percent, in Spain it was down 11.7 percent and in Portugal consumption fell a hefty 19.5 percent. The Spanish and Portuguese fall in demand was mainly because a three-year drought in the Iberian peninsula ended in 1996 and boosted hydro electric power.

Forecasts for Spanish demand are not available from the IEA but Peter Bogin of Cambridge Energy Research Associates in Paris said he saw gas displacing around half of Spain's and Portugal's fuel oil consumption by the turn of the century.

The U.K.'s fuel consumption was 12.5 percent down in 1996 due to the relentess drive of gas into the power market. U.K. consumption of natural gas rose by 20 percent in 1996 and outpaced that of oil for the first time in history.
Calculated on an energy-equivalent basis against fuel oil, natural gas in the U.K. is currently worth around $60 per tonne, the analyst said. This compares with high sulphur fuel oil at around $80.
The vagueries of winter weather always provide a wild card when forecasting fuel oil demand and stop-start Russian exports make short-term supply forecasts difficult.

Russian fuel exports from the Baltics and the Black Sea were around a million tonnes in January and February, nearly triple the levels of a year ago when an export ban was in place. But Russian fuel oil output is unlikely to change before the turn of the millennium.
Boston Consulting group said recently it foresees extra cracking capacity in place in Russia by the year 2,000.

"You will clearly increase light products capacity, but you also at least maintain the heavy products," Boston consulting group Vice-President Charbel Ackermann said. "It is not a substitution or a reduction of heavy capacity."
